prompt: Match each field type to the value a new object's field of that type starts with.
hint: The zero of each type.

prompt: `Member` declares `int maxLoans = 3;`. After `other.maxLoans = 5;`, what is `m.maxLoans` for a different member `m`?
hint: Each object has its own copy.

choices.why: Right: the initialiser gave each member 3, and the assignment changed only `other`'s.

choices.text: 5, because the assignment changes the initialiser for every member
choices.why: An assignment changes one object's field; the initialiser in the class is untouched.

choices.text: 0, the default of an `int`
choices.why: The initialiser beats the default, so every new member starts at 3.

prompt: Why did `Defaults` print `(int) m.tier` rather than `m.tier`?
hint: What does the character with code 0 look like?

choices.text: A `char` cannot be printed without a cast
choices.why: `println` prints a `char` as a character quite happily; this one is simply invisible.

choices.text: Without the cast it would print `null`
choices.why: `char` is a primitive, so it is never `null`.

choices.text: Code 0 prints as nothing visible; the number shows it
choices.why: Right: as a character the line would look empty; as a number it says 0.

choices.text: The cast turns the field into an `int` from that line on, for good
choices.why: A cast converts one value in one expression; the field stays a `char`.

prompt: A local variable read before it is assigned is a compile error, and a field read before it is assigned is `0` or `null`. Why the difference?
hint: Think about what the compiler can see.

choices.text: Fields are less important, so the compiler checks them less strictly
choices.why: It is not about importance; the check is impossible for a field.

choices.text: A local lives in one method the compiler reads; a field is set from anywhere, so the JVM zeroes it
choices.why: Right: no check follows every method that sets a field, so the safe default is zero.

choices.text: Locals live on the heap, where the memory of a new frame is never cleared before the method uses it
choices.why: It is the other way round: objects, and their fields, live on the heap, and new objects are cleared.

prompt: In `int maxLoans = 3;` declared in a class, the `= 3` part is called an ___.
hint: It runs for every new object.

prompt: Inside `describe()`, `title` is written with no dot before it. Whose title is it?
hint: A method runs on one object.

choices.text: The title of the last book created
choices.why: No class keeps track of its last object; the method uses the one it was called on.

choices.text: The title of the book before the dot in the call
choices.why: Right: in `b.describe()`, it is `b`'s book.

choices.text: A local variable `describe` declares, which starts as `null`
choices.why: `describe` declares no local; `title` with no dot is the field.

choices.text: Every book's title, joined together
choices.why: A method runs on one object, not on all of them.

prompt: What does `void` before `lend()` say?
hint: `WrongCall` tried to use its result.

choices.text: That the method changes nothing
choices.why: `lend` changes `timesLent`; `void` is about what it gives back.

choices.text: That the method may be called only once per object
choices.why: `b.lend()` ran twice and `timesLent` reached 2.

choices.text: That it gives nothing back
choices.why: Right: so `String nothing = b.lend();` did not compile.

choices.text: That it takes no parameters
choices.why: The empty brackets say that; `void` is the return type.

prompt: In `void rename(String title) { this.title = title; }`, what would `title = title;` do instead?
hint: Which `title` wins inside the method?

choices.text: The same, since Java works out which one is the field
choices.why: Inside the method the plain name means the parameter, on both sides.

choices.text: Assign the parameter to itself and leave the field unchanged
choices.why: Right: the parameter hides the field, and section 04's `Copy` printed `null` for this reason.

choices.text: Fail to compile, because a name is used twice
choices.why: It compiles without a warning, which is what makes it dangerous.

prompt: Which of these is the signature of `isOlderThan`, as the compiler keeps it?
hint: `javap -p` printed it.

choices.text: `boolean isOlderThan`
choices.why: That is the return type and the name; the parameter types are missing.

choices.text: `isOlderThan(otherYear)`
choices.why: The parameter's name is not part of the signature; its type is.

choices.text: `isOlderThan(int)`
choices.why: Right: the name and the parameter types.

choices.text: `isOlderThan(int otherYear) -> boolean`
choices.why: Java writes no arrow, and neither the parameter name nor the return type belong to the signature.

prompt: `timesLent` starts at 0. `UseBook` called `b.lend()` twice. What did it print for `b.timesLent`?
hint: Each call adds one.

prompt: `Book` has `boolean isOlderThan(int otherYear)`. Which calls compile? Choose all that apply.
hint: The argument must be an `int`, and the result is a `boolean`.

choices.text: `boolean old = b.isOlderThan(1900);`
choices.why: Yes: an `int` in, a `boolean` out.

choices.text: `boolean old = b.isOlderThan("1900");`
choices.why: No: `"1900"` is a `String`, the first error in `WrongCall`.

choices.text: `System.out.println(b.isOlderThan(b.year + 1));`
choices.why: Yes: `b.year + 1` is an `int`, and `println` accepts a `boolean`.

choices.text: `int n = b.isOlderThan(1900);`
choices.why: No: the result is a `boolean`, and an `int` cannot hold one.

prompt: How does a constructor's declaration differ from a method's?
hint: Look at `Book(String isbn, String title, int year)`.

choices.text: It must take at least one parameter
choices.why: A constructor may take none; the compiler's own `Book()` took none.

choices.text: Its name is the class's name, and it declares no return type
choices.why: Right: not even `void`.

choices.text: It is declared outside the class body, after the closing brace
choices.why: It sits inside the class, beside the fields and the methods.

choices.text: It returns the new object with `return this;`
choices.why: A constructor has no `return` value; `new` hands the object back.

prompt: After the two constructors were added to `Book`, `new Book()` stopped compiling. Why?
hint: Lessons 1 and 12 met a constructor nobody wrote.

choices.text: The compiler adds `Book()` only to a class that declares no constructor
choices.why: Right: declare one and the free one is gone, as `javap -p` confirmed.

choices.text: `new` needs at least one argument once a class has fields
choices.why: Lesson 12's `Book` had fields and `new Book()` worked; what changed was the declared constructors.

choices.text: `this(...)` in the second constructor deletes the first
choices.why: Both constructors are in `javap`'s listing; `this(...)` calls one, it removes nothing.

prompt: `Book(String isbn, String title) { this(isbn, title, 0); }` — what does `this(...)` do here?
hint: It is not `this.` with a dot.

choices.text: It makes a second `Book` with year 0 and returns it
choices.why: No second object is made; the same object goes through the other constructor.

choices.text: It sets a field called `this` to the three values
choices.why: There is no such field; `this(...)` is a call.

choices.text: Runs the three-argument constructor on this same object
choices.why: Right: the storing is written once, and the two-argument version supplies 0 for the year.

prompt: `Copy(String barcode) { barcode = barcode; }` compiles, and `new Copy("BC-0001").barcode` is `null`. Which change makes it print `BC-0001`?
hint: Only one side of the assignment is the field.

choices.text: `barcode = this.barcode;`
choices.why: That copies the field, still `null`, into the parameter: the wrong direction.

choices.text: `this.barcode = barcode;`
choices.why: Right: the field on the left, the parameter on the right.

choices.text: Declare the field as `String barcode = "";`
choices.why: The field would start as an empty string and the assignment would still miss it.

choices.text: Compile with `javac -g`, which keeps the names apart
choices.why: `-g` keeps names for messages; it changes no meaning.

prompt: `new Book("978-85-01-01234-5", "Untitled draft")` runs. Put what happens in order.
hint: The two-argument constructor hands over to the three-argument one.
items: The object is made with every field at its default
The two-argument constructor starts and calls `this(isbn, title, 0)`
The three-argument constructor stores the ISBN, the title and the year 0
`new` hands the reference back to `main`, into `b`

prompt: When a constructor's parameter has the same name as a field, the field is reached as `___.barcode`.
hint: It names the object being built.

prompt: A class `Loan` declares `Loan(Book book, Member member)` and nothing else. A colleague writes `Loan l = new Loan(); l.book = b;`. What does `javac` do?
hint: Section 04's `OldMain`.

choices.text: Compiles it, and `l.member` stays `null`
choices.why: It never gets that far: there is no constructor with no arguments.

choices.text: Refuses it, listing `Loan(Book,Member)` as the constructor that does not fit
choices.why: Right: declaring a constructor removed the free one, which is how the class forces both values in.

choices.text: Warns, then adds an empty constructor for this one call
choices.why: The compiler adds the free constructor only when the class declares none, and it never adds one on demand.

prompt: Which belongs in a method of `Book` rather than in `main`?
hint: Behaviour goes beside the data it works on.

choices.text: Choosing which books to make when the program starts
choices.why: That is the program's job; a book does not know which other books exist.

choices.text: Reading the title the user types at the keyboard
choices.why: Input belongs to the program around the books, not to one book.

choices.text: Adding one to the count of times this book was lent
choices.why: Right: `lend()` changes this book's `timesLent`, so the rule lives in one place.

prompt: Which of these always runs exactly once for every `Book` that `new` makes?
hint: The others run only when somebody calls them.

choices.text: `describe()`
choices.why: A method runs when it is called, any number of times, including none.

choices.text: One of its constructors
choices.why: Right: `new` always runs one, chosen by the arguments.

choices.text: `main`, once per object made
choices.why: `main` runs once per program, when the JVM starts it.

choices.text: `lend()`, to set `timesLent` to its default
choices.why: The default is set by the JVM clearing the memory; `lend` adds one when called.
